transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um… I’m here because I can’t really stop noticing my face, especially on these lesson videos we record. One side looks crooked to me, kind of swollen-looking, and once I see it I can’t unsee it.

And then I start thinking the students are noticing it, or parents if they watch the clips, or other staff… like they’re staring at that instead of listening to what I’m saying. Which is ridiculous maybe, because I’m supposed to be teaching, and I’ll be explaining something about exams or whatever, but in my head I’m just thinking, “That’s what they’re looking at.” It’s become really hard to get past.
Is it always your face that you're concerned about, or are there other parts of your body that you worry about as well?

It’s mainly my face, yeah… well, the one side of it. I keep seeing it on the lesson videos, like it looks crooked or swollen somehow, and then I’m not even thinking about the lesson anymore.

I’ll be trying to explain something to the class, and then my mind goes to, you know, if a parent watches this later or another teacher sees it, they must be noticing that side of my face instead of what I’m saying. It’s not really, like, my arms or my body or anything. It’s that face thing on the recordings.
Do these thoughts about your face pop into your head when you're not trying to think about them?

Yeah… it does. I mean, I’ll be trying not to think about it, like I’ll be setting up a lesson or just checking the recording for something completely normal, and suddenly I see that one side of my face looking crooked or swollen and then it’s just… there.

And then I’m thinking, are the students seeing that? If parents watch the video later, are they staring at that instead of hearing what I’m saying? Even staff, if they come across it. It sort of takes over, even when I’m supposed to be focused on teaching.
Are these thoughts about your face interfering with your ability to teach or interact with your students and colleagues?

Yeah… it is. I mean, I keep telling myself I’m still doing the job, because I’m in the classroom and I’m talking to them, but everything around it is slipping.

Lesson planning takes me forever now, or I don’t finish it on time, because I get caught up checking how I look in the videos or avoiding doing things that might be recorded. And then mentoring students, and even basketball coaching after school… I used to be on top of all that, but now I’m behind on all of it.

The administrators have started writing things down, like missed deadlines and when I couldn’t cover things properly. Sorry, I’m rambling — there was one timetable change last week and normally I’d just handle it, but I got stuck worrying about a clip someone might see. So yeah… it’s affecting work a lot. I’m honestly scared I’m getting close to losing my position.
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over to try to make yourself feel better about how your face looks?

Yeah… I do. More than I want to admit, probably.

Like before I post a recorded lesson, I’ll keep moving the camera—higher, lower, turned a bit—then I replay the clip, and replay it again, just looking at that side of my face instead of checking the actual lesson. Sometimes I’ll kind of hold my hand near my cheek or jaw, like casually, but really I’m trying to cover it.

And with parent conferences on video, it’s worse because I feel like they’re just staring at me while I’m trying to talk about their kid’s coursework. I’ll re-record a whole lesson if I think it looks bad, even if the explanation was fine. Then suddenly I’ve lost an hour, or more, and I haven’t prepped the next class properly, and I’m rushing in late or behind.

It sounds ridiculous saying it out loud, but yeah, I keep doing those things over and over to try to make it feel okay.
Do you think something bad would happen if you didn't keep checking and re-recording your lessons?

Yeah… I mean, it feels like something bad would happen, even if I know that sounds dramatic.

Like if I don’t check the clip again, or don’t move the camera a bit, then I imagine it’ll go out with my face looking… wrong, and then students will notice, or parents will see it in a conference and just focus on that. So I end up changing the angle over and over, replaying the same part, sometimes putting my hand near my face like I’m just thinking, but really I’m hiding it.

And then, sorry, this is a bit off, but even when I’m supposed to be prepping the next class, I’ll still be stuck on the recording. I’ve re-recorded whole lessons because of it, and then I’m late or I haven’t finished what I needed for the next group. So yeah, I guess I do feel like if I don’t do it, something will be out there and I won’t be able to fix it.
Is it always the same specific issue with your face that bothers you, like it being crooked or swollen, or do you find yourself worrying about different aspects of your appearance at different times?

It’s mostly the same thing, I think… that one side of my face. On the lesson videos it looks crooked to me, kind of swollen, and once I see it I can’t unsee it.

I’ll be trying to explain something about an assignment, and instead I’m just thinking, “That’s all they’re looking at.” Like the students, or their parents, or even other staff if they watch it — I feel like they must be staring at that side of my face instead of hearing anything I’m saying.

I mean, sometimes I’ll get distracted by the lighting or the angle too, but it all comes back to that same side looking wrong. Sorry, I know you asked if it changes… it’s mainly that.
Do you think you would still be bothered by the appearance of your face if you were certain that no one else noticed or cared about it?

I think… yeah, probably. I mean, it’s hard to separate it, because the whole thing starts when I see it on the lesson videos and then I immediately imagine the students or parents noticing it too.

But even if you told me no one cared, I’d still see that one side of my face looking crooked or swollen, and it would still pull my attention away from what I’m actually trying to say. Like I’ll be explaining coursework, but my brain is just stuck on, “That looks wrong.”

Sorry, I know that’s not exactly a straight answer. I guess the answer is yes — I’d still be bothered, but it gets much worse when I think other people must be staring at it instead of listening.
Do you think you would feel better about your face if you could somehow prove to yourself that it looks normal?

I think I’d want that to make me feel better, yeah… like if there was some way to prove it looked normal, maybe I’d calm down for a bit.

But the problem is, when I see myself on the lesson videos, I can’t stop seeing that one side of my face as crooked or sort of swollen-looking. And then I’m not even thinking about the lesson anymore — I’m thinking the students, or their parents, or other staff must be staring at it instead of listening to what I’m saying.

Sorry, I know that’s not exactly what you asked. I suppose even if someone proved it to me, I’d still be checking the video and thinking, “But it looks wrong there.”
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and re-record your lessons if you were teaching in a classroom without any video recordings?

I suppose if there weren’t any video recordings, the re-recording part wouldn’t happen, obviously. In a classroom I’d probably still think about how my face looks, but the checking is really tied to the camera.

Before I post a recorded lesson, I keep messing with the angle and replaying clips, and sometimes I put my hand over part of my face to see if that side looks as bad as I think it does. It’s stupid because I’ll mean to just check one bit, then suddenly I’ve watched it over and over and I’m late doing prep.

It’s the same with parent conferences if they’re on camera — I’ll adjust the camera, move it higher, lower, turn the light on, turn it off… and then I’m thinking about my face instead of the actual meeting. So, without video, maybe not in the same way. But the video makes it much worse because I can keep checking it.
Do you think people would judge you differently as a person if they saw the side of your face that you're concerned about?

Yeah… I think they would, or at least I’m afraid they would. Like, if they saw that side of my face looking crooked or swollen on the lesson videos, I feel like they’d stop listening to what I’m actually teaching and just think, “What’s wrong with his face?”

And then I start imagining the students noticing it, or parents watching the recording and judging me, or staff seeing it and thinking I look odd. I know I’m supposed to be focused on the lesson content — I’ll be explaining something completely normal, like coursework deadlines or whatever — but once I notice it, that’s all I can think about.

So yes, I suppose I do worry they’d judge me differently, not just notice it. Like it would change how they see me as a teacher.
Do you think you would still feel anxious about your face if you believed people liked and accepted you as a teacher, regardless of your appearance?

I think… maybe it would help a bit if I really believed they accepted me as a teacher. Like, if I knew the students and parents weren’t judging my teaching because of it.

But I don’t think it would stop the anxiety, because I’m here because I can’t stop seeing that crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on the lesson videos. Once I notice it, it’s like everything else drops away. I’ll be trying to listen to what I’m saying in the lesson, and instead I’m staring at that side of my face and thinking everyone else must be staring at it too.

Sorry, that’s not really about being liked, is it? I just mean… even if they liked me, I think I’d still get stuck on how it looks.
Do you think your anxiety about your face would decrease if you were certain that everyone who saw you liked and accepted you, not just as a teacher, but as a person?

Maybe a little, but… I don’t think it would go away. Because the problem is, once I see that side of my face on a video, the crooked, swollen-looking bit, I can’t unsee it.

Even if everyone said they liked me as a person, I’d still be sitting there replaying the lesson and thinking, “They must be looking at that instead of listening.” Students, parents, staff… it just feels like it would pull their attention straight to my face.

Sorry, I know you’re asking about being accepted, but my mind goes straight back to the recordings. Like I can know, in theory, people aren’t being cruel, but when I see it on screen it feels obvious. Then I can’t focus on anything I’m saying.
Do you think you would still feel the need to hide or fix your face if you were alone in a room with no one to see you?

If I was completely alone… I suppose I’d still feel it, but it’s worst when I know someone’s going to see it. Like before I upload a recorded lesson or join a parent conference, that’s when I really start messing about with it.

I’ll move the camera angle slightly, then replay the clip, then pause it and think, “No, that side looks wrong.” Sometimes I’ll sort of cover part of my face with my hand without even meaning to, just to see if it looks less noticeable. And then I’ll re-record the whole thing, even if the explanation was fine.

Sorry, I’m going off a bit. It’s just… it eats up loads of time. I’ve missed prep work because I’m still checking the video, and then I’m late getting to classes or behind on what I’m supposed to be doing. So if no one could see me, maybe I wouldn’t be as frantic, but I still get caught in trying to fix how it looks.
Do you think you would still be concerned about the appearance of your face if you were certain that it was perfectly symmetrical and normal-looking?

If I was certain it was perfectly symmetrical and normal-looking… I suppose that would change things, yes. But that’s the part I can’t really get to.

Because I’m here because I can’t stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on the lesson videos. I’ll be trying to check whether the explanation was clear, or whether the class could hear me properly, and then I just lock onto that side of my face. And once I’ve seen it, it’s like I can’t believe anyone else wouldn’t see it too.

Like students, parents, other staff if they watch something back… I start thinking they must be staring at that instead of listening to anything I’m saying. So if I truly knew it was normal-looking, maybe I wouldn’t be so caught up in it. But right now, when I see the videos, it doesn’t feel normal to me at all.
Do you think your concerns about your face would decrease if you were certain that everyone who saw you thought you looked completely normal, but you still saw the flaw yourself?

I think… maybe it would decrease a bit if I knew they all thought I looked normal. But I don’t think it would stop, because I’d still be the one seeing it.

That’s sort of the problem, really. I’m here because I can’t stop noticing that crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on the lesson videos. I’ll mean to watch back whether the lesson made sense, and then suddenly I’m not listening to myself at all, I’m just staring at that bit of my face.

And then even if you told me, “No, everyone thinks you look completely normal,” I’d still think… well, how? How are they not seeing it? Students, parents, staff, whoever watches it — I’d still feel like their eyes must go straight there instead of to what I’m saying.

Sorry, I know that’s not exactly a straight answer. I suppose yes, being sure they thought I looked normal might help a little, but if I could still see the flaw myself, I’d still be stuck on it.
Do you think your anxiety about your face would be the same if you never showed your face to anyone?

If I never showed my face to anyone… I think it might take some pressure off, yes. But I don’t know that it would just disappear.

It’s the videos that really set me off. I’m here because I can’t stop seeing that crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on them. I’ll be meant to check the lesson, and then I’m not even hearing what I’m saying anymore, I’m just staring at my face.

And then my mind goes to the students, or parents, or other staff watching it, and I think they must be looking at that instead of listening to the lesson. If no one ever saw my face, maybe that part would be less intense… but I’d still know what it looks like to me, if that makes sense.
Do you think you would still feel compelled to check and re-record your lessons if you were the only one who would ever see them?

I think… yes, probably. Maybe not as badly if no one else was going to see them, but I’d still check them.

Before I post a lesson, I get caught in this whole routine with the camera angle — moving it a bit, then watching it back, then thinking one side of my face looks wrong, so I try again. Sometimes I’ll cover part of my face with my hand while I’m watching, just to see if it looks less noticeable, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud.

And it’s not just lessons, it happens before parent conferences too. I’ll be adjusting the camera and replaying little clips instead of just getting on with it. I’ve re-recorded entire lessons because I couldn’t stand how my face looked, and then I end up missing prep work or being late for classes, which is… not exactly helping anything.

Sorry, I’m going off a bit. If I was truly the only one seeing them, maybe the urgency would be less, but I think I’d still feel pulled to check and fix it.
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and re-record your lessons if you were certain that no one would ever judge you based on your appearance?

I think I would still feel the need, yes. Maybe I’d tell myself it didn’t matter if no one was judging me, but once I see it on the screen, I can’t seem to leave it alone.

Before I post a recorded lesson, or even before a parent conference, I’ll keep shifting the camera angle and replaying little clips. Sometimes I cover part of my face with my hand to see if it looks better or less obvious, which… I know sounds strange. And then I’ll think, no, that angle is wrong, or that side of my face looks too off, and I’ll record it again.

It can go on so long that I miss prep work, or I end up late with classes. So if no one judged me, maybe I’d be less panicked about it, but I think I’d still keep checking and re-recording because I’d still see it.
Would you still feel the need to check and re-record your lessons if you were certain that your face appeared perfectly normal to everyone who saw it?

I think… even then, I’d probably still do it. That’s the annoying thing. If someone told me, completely honestly, “Your face looks normal to everyone,” I’d want to believe them, but when I’m looking at the video, I get stuck.

Before I post a lesson, or before a parent conference, I’ll keep moving the camera angle around and watching little bits back. Then I’ll cover part of my face with my hand, like I’m testing whether it looks less noticeable, and then I think, no, the lighting’s wrong, or that side looks strange, and I start again.

Sometimes I re-record the whole thing so many times that I’ve lost the time I needed for prep, and then I’m rushing or late to class. Which is stupid, because the lesson content is what should matter — I mean, I had one Year 10 group where the sound wasn’t even great and they still understood it, so clearly I know that in theory. But in the moment, if I can see my face on the screen, I don’t seem to be able to just leave it.
